text: Chapter 1 introduced distributed tracing in the abstract: one trace ID, shared spans across services, reconstructing a request's full path. This lesson ties that directly to AWS X-Ray — segments, subsegments, the service map X-Ray builds for you automatically, and the sampling rules that decide which requests get traced at all.

A segment is the record of one service's own work on a request — start time, end time, HTTP status, any errors. A subsegment nests inside it as a finer breakdown: a call out to DynamoDB, a call to another downstream service, a block of code you wrapped explicitly. Every segment and subsegment belonging to one request shares a single trace ID, and X-Ray assembles all of them, across every service touched, into one reconstructed timeline.

Two separate pieces make that happen. The X-Ray SDK lives inside your application code and creates segments and subsegments as requests run — available for Node.js, Python, Java, and more. The X-Ray daemon is a small background process, running as a sidecar, a DaemonSet on EKS, or built into the Lambda execution environment, that batches completed segment data to the X-Ray API over UDP. Your application never calls that API directly, so instrumenting a request never adds API latency to the request being measured.

Because every segment already records its own service and its downstream calls, X-Ray assembles a service map automatically — a graph of every service seen in recent traces, the calls between them, and per-edge average latency and error rate. On a real incident, that map is often the fastest place to look: a node colored for elevated errors tells you immediately which service actually degraded, before you open a single trace to find out why.

Tracing every request in a high-traffic service wastes storage and API calls on requests that are completely unremarkable. X-Ray's default sampling rule traces the first request each second plus 5% of anything beyond that. Custom sampling rules override this by service, method, or path, with their own reservoir — a guaranteed number of traces per second — and a fixed rate beyond it, so checkout traffic gets meaningfully traced while noisy health-check pings get traced almost never.

That's X-Ray: segments and subsegments record the work, the SDK and daemon move that data off the request path, the service map turns it into a topology you never drew by hand, and sampling rules control the cost of tracing at real production volume. Next lesson applies CloudWatch itself to Kubernetes, with Container Insights surfacing cluster, node, pod, and container metrics for EKS workloads.
